row.note: The commentary makes salvation turn on what a person does rather than a named lineage; John refuses reliance on Abrahamic descent and demands fruit worthy of repentance.

row.basis: God repays each according to deeds
row.note: The commentary hears kad eflaha as a completed verdict; Paul says God repays each person according to deeds, making the judgment individual and conclusive.
The commentary's men leaves the subject open to anyone who purifies themself; Paul grounds judgment in God's impartiality across persons.

row.basis: Break fallow ground and sow righteousness
row.note: The commentary joins f-l-h's plowing image to t-z-k-w's growth; Hosea tells Israel to break fallow ground, sow righteousness, and seek the Lord until he rains righteousness.
The commentary pictures cultivation opening resistant soil for growth; Jeremiah uses the same field work as an appeal to prepare the heart and stop sowing among thorns.
Jeremiah follows the call to break fallow ground with removing the heart's foreskin; this makes the field image an inward moral transformation, not merely crop language.
The commentary allows tezekkâ to mean giving as well as purification; Jesus connects giving alms from within with everything becoming clean.
The commentary reads tezekkâ as taking purification upon oneself; John says everyone with hope in God purifies themself, tying hope to active moral change.
The commentary presents purification as a person's sustained work; Paul tells the community to work out its salvation with fear and trembling.
The commentary also says the person's purification rests on ground God prepared; Paul immediately says God is at work in them, joining human effort to divine enabling.
The commentary joins cleansing with crop growth; Jesus describes the Father pruning the fruitful branch so that it bears more fruit, making purification productive.
The commentary links giving, growth, and felâh; Paul says the one who sows generously will reap generously, applying the crop image to giving.
The commentary says giving can make the giver grow; Paul says God supplies seed and increases the harvest of righteousness, placing increase under divine agency.
The commentary places purification before prayer; Exodus requires priests to wash hands and feet before entering the tent or approaching the altar, under penalty of death.
The commentary's purified person then remembers God and prays; the psalm describes the worshipper who may ascend the Lord's hill as clean-handed and pure-hearted.
Isaiah makes cleansing an active turning from evil, matching the commentary's distinction between undertaking purification and merely claiming to be pure.

row.basis: Learn good and defend the vulnerable
row.note: The commentary treats purification as a lived action; Isaiah spells out that change as learning good, seeking justice, and defending the oppressed.

row.basis: Almsgiving purges sin and saves from death
row.note: The commentary hears tezekkâ as both purification and giving; Raphael says almsgiving purges sin and saves from death, joining generosity to deliverance.
The commentary links purification with giving from one's wealth; Sirach says almsgiving atones for sin, a direct Jewish wisdom formulation of that connection.

row.basis: Fruits now and principal in the world to come
row.note: The commentary contrasts transient present life with felâh as lasting good; the Mishnah says some deeds bear fruit in this world while their principal remains for the world to come.

The commentary holds human purification together with God's prior enabling; the Community Rule describes God purifying a person from wickedness by a holy spirit, giving that relation a sectarian Jewish form.

row.basis: Moses calls Pharaoh to humble himself
row.note: The commentary reads Qur'an 79:18-19 as an invitation for Pharaoh to purify himself and fear God; Moses here asks Pharaoh to humble himself before the Lord during the plagues, but the story proceeds through refusal rather than accepted purification.

row.basis: Pharaoh exalts himself against the people
row.note: The commentary rejects worldly superiority as the measure of felâh; Exodus names Pharaoh's self-exaltation against God's people as the posture under judgment.
The commentary's men makes the successful person one who acts, not one who belongs to a group; Paul promises glory and peace to everyone who does good, Jew and Greek.
The commentary distinguishes a person's verbal claim to purity from God's verdict; the Pharisee's prayer lists his own righteousness and compares himself favorably with others.

row.basis: The tax collector asks for mercy
row.note: The commentary says the person purified does not pronounce the final judgment on themself; the tax collector asks God for mercy rather than declaring his own purity.
The commentary's kad eflaha is a verdict stated by God about the person; Jesus says the humbled tax collector, not the self-exalting Pharisee, goes home justified.
The commentary links giving to a lasting divine reward; Jesus says the Father who sees hidden almsgiving will repay it.

row.basis: Prayer and alms as a memorial
row.note: The commentary completes purification with remembering God and prayer; Cornelius's prayers and alms rise together as a memorial before God.
The commentary contrasts present preference with what lasts; Jesus joins selling possessions and giving alms to treasure that does not fail.

row.basis: Sowing to the Spirit and eternal life
row.note: The commentary combines agricultural growth with felâh as lasting good; Paul contrasts sowing to the Spirit, which reaps eternal life, with corruption.
The commentary describes purification as a state gained through effort; Paul urges persistence in doing good because harvest comes in its season.
The commentary's success belongs to the one who undertakes the work of purification; James warns against hearing the word without doing it.
The commentary connects purification to giving and a transformed life; James calls care for orphans and widows and keeping unstained from the world pure religion.
The commentary places purification before prayer; Hebrews urges drawing near with a true heart, hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed.
The commentary describes tezekkâ as taking purification upon oneself; Paul says anyone who cleanses themself becomes set apart and ready for every good work.
The commentary says self-purification occurs on ground God has prepared; Deuteronomy says God circumcises Israel's heart so they can love him, making divine enablement prior to human response.
The commentary treats purification as real change rather than self-praise; Ezekiel promises God's cleansing of the people from their impurities.
The commentary holds human effort together with God's ordering and guidance; Ezekiel's promise of a new heart and spirit identifies God as the source of renewed conduct.
The commentary places purification before worship; Leviticus says the people are cleansed from sin on the Day of Atonement before the Lord.
The commentary links purification to remembrance and prayer; Malachi's refiner purifies the sons of Levi so their offerings can be presented in righteousness.
The commentary describes giving as a form of growth despite apparent decrease; Proverbs says the generous person is enriched and one who refreshes others is refreshed.

The source commentary labels the Arabic root z-k-w; Job uses Hebrew z-k-h to ask whether a human can be pure before God, a cognate usage framed as a question about divine judgment rather than a claim of self-purity.

The source commentary gives Arabic f-l-h the lexical gloss of plowing or splitting behind success; Psalm 141 depicts a plowman cleaving earth, a plausible cognate agrarian use that does not equate plowing with salvation.
The commentary's plowed soil receives water and yields a crop, while felâh includes lasting good; the righteous in this psalm are a tree by water that bears fruit and does not wither.
The commentary contrasts productive growth with vegetation that becomes dry refuse; the psalm's wicked are chaff driven away, the opposite fate of the rooted tree.

row.basis: A clean heart created by God
row.note: The commentary distinguishes self-purification from declaring oneself pure and says God prepares the ground; the psalmist asks God to create a clean heart, making purification dependent on divine action.

row.basis: Grass fades but God's word endures
row.note: The commentary contrasts short-lived worldly life with what is better and more lasting; Isaiah sets withering grass against the word of God that stands forever.
The commentary contrasts unending punishment without life with a lasting good; Daniel distinguishes those who awaken to everlasting life from those facing shame.
The commentary hears the past-tense success declaration as a settled judgment; Daniel's writing on the wall says the king was weighed and found deficient, a contrary verdict after his deeds.
The commentary says the lasting outcome is chosen through present action; Avot calls this world a vestibule and urges preparation here for the world to come.

row.basis: Good deeds now and life to come
row.note: The commentary makes the afterlife more enduring than present life; Avot says an hour of repentance and good deeds in this world outweighs the whole life to come, while future bliss exceeds this world's life.
The commentary joins purification, giving, and prayer to the final outcome; the Talmud says charity, prayer, and change of deeds can tear up a decree.
The commentary places purification before the act of prayer; the pious in this Mishnah wait an hour before praying, an interpretive practice of inward preparation.
The commentary distinguishes undertaken purification from appearance or self-claim; Jesus condemns vessels cleaned outside but filled within with greed and self-indulgence.
The commentary places inner purification before outward worship; Jesus says to clean the inside first so the outside may become clean too.
The commentary moves from admonition heard to purification and then prayer; Jesus's good soil receives the word and bears fruit, with differing yields.
The commentary associates felâh with remaining in good; Jesus says the branch must abide in the vine to bear fruit, linking fruitfulness to continued attachment.
The commentary describes human cultivation but says the crop's growth belongs to God; Paul says one planted and another watered, but God gave the growth.
The commentary refuses to make the human worker the source of the crop; Paul says neither planter nor waterer is anything, but God who gives growth.
The commentary connects crop growth with a lasting outcome; Paul uses seed language for resurrection, contrasting what is sown perishable with what is raised imperishable.

row.basis: Fruit that ends in eternal life
row.note: The commentary's crop image and felâh's permanence meet in Paul's sequence of freedom from sin, fruit for holiness, and the end of eternal life.
The commentary makes purification an action rather than a group label; James argues that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone, making deed and verdict explicit.
The commentary contrasts inward purification with mere outward cleansing; Peter says baptism is not removal of dirt from the body but an appeal to God for a good conscience.
The commentary says human purification takes place on ground first prepared by God; Paul says believers are God's workmanship, created for good works prepared beforehand.
The commentary presents success as an already declared result of a person's action; Christ comes with recompense to repay each according to their work.
The commentary says felâh means reaching what one seeks and remaining in good; Paul compares disciplined effort to a race in which runners strive to obtain the prize.
The commentary describes punishment as a continuing state that is neither life nor death; Jesus's image of the undying worm and unquenched fire gives a related picture of unending punishment.
The commentary links giving and crop increase; Proverbs asks Israel to honor the Lord with wealth and firstfruits, followed by barns filled with plenty, a material rather than afterlife promise.
The commentary makes the outcome depend on the person's own turning rather than ancestry; Ezekiel says the wicked person who turns, practices justice, and keeps the statutes will live.

The commentary treats purification as an effortful state and felâh as arrival at lasting good; Paul describes those who persist in doing good while seeking glory, honor, and immortality, and promises eternal life.
The commentary connects admonition with a person's own purification; Paul says he called people to repent, turn to God, and perform deeds worthy of repentance.
The commentary makes purification the defining act before the promised outcome; Jesus links purity of heart to seeing God.

row.basis: The final verdict and acts of mercy
row.note: The commentary's success is a verdict about what a person has done; the king's judgment identifies feeding and caring for the vulnerable as deeds done to him.
The commentary describes tezekkâ as taking purification upon oneself; Paul urges believers to cleanse themselves from defilement and bring holiness to completion in reverence for God.
The commentary links purification with the deeds of a person's life; Titus says Christ purifies a people for himself who are eager to do good works.
The commentary presents purification as an active undertaking; Peter says the readers have purified their souls through obedience to the truth, leading to sincere love.

row.basis: Wash sins while calling on the name
row.note: The commentary places purification before remembering the Lord's name and praying; Ananias tells Paul to be baptized, wash away his sins, and call on Jesus's name.
The commentary joins giving with prayer and remembrance of God; Hebrews says doing good and sharing are sacrifices that please God.
The commentary contrasts present preference with the more enduring hereafter; Paul tells the rich to be generous and share, thereby storing treasure for the future and grasping true life.

The commentary describes punishment as a state in which one neither dies nor lives; Isaiah depicts the corpses of rebels with a worm that does not die and a fire that is not quenched, supplying a close but materially different image of unending punishment.
The commentary allows purification to carry the sense of giving; Isaiah describes the fast God chooses as sharing bread and shelter with the needy, making piety an act toward others.

row.basis: Light and healing after just giving
row.note: The commentary's crop image associates fruitful action with growth; Isaiah says light breaks like dawn and healing springs up after the just fast and care for the needy.

row.basis: Those who fear and remember the divine name
row.note: The commentary links the person who fears the reminder with the one who remembers the Lord's name; Malachi places those who fear the Lord and esteem his name in a book of remembrance, anticipating divine judgment.

row.basis: God sees changed deeds and relents
row.note: The commentary makes the announced outcome depend on a person's action; Jonah says God saw Nineveh's deeds, that they turned from evil, and relented from the announced calamity.

row.basis: Giving to the poor as a loan to God
row.note: The commentary hears tezekkâ as giving whose apparent loss becomes increase; Proverbs says one who is gracious to the poor lends to the Lord, who repays the deed.
The commentary places the lived act of purification before remembrance and prayer; Samuel says obedience to God's voice is better than sacrifice, making ritual service answer to prior conduct.
The commentary locates purification in what a person undertakes; Micah says what God requires is to do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with God, rather than naming a lineage or ritual.

row.basis: Sowing in tears and reaping joy
row.note: The commentary develops cultivation as effort followed by yield; the psalm promises that those who sow in tears will reap in joy, joining costly action to its later outcome.
The commentary associates plowing and growth with divine provision; Isaac sows in the land and reaps a hundredfold because the Lord blesses him.
The commentary describes felâh as reaching a sought good and remaining in it; Proverbs says the one who pursues righteousness and kindness finds life, righteousness, and honor.
The commentary describes purification as a state developed through effort; Proverbs compares the righteous path to dawn growing brighter until full day.
The commentary notes cleansing before prayer; the Talmud's morning blessings include a blessing over washing the hands, placing bodily cleansing within preparation for worship.

row.basis: The righteous are in God's hand after death
row.note: The commentary opposes the punishment that is neither life nor death with lasting good; Wisdom says the souls of the righteous are in God's hand and that they are at peace despite appearances of death.
The commentary connects purification with growth and the offering of worship; Wisdom says God tested the righteous like gold in a furnace and accepted them as a sacrificial offering.
The commentary rejects the claim that worldly superiority defines success; James says God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble.

row.basis: Praise and confession of the name
row.note: The commentary's purified person remembers the Lord's name and prays; Hebrews describes praise and confession of Jesus's name as a continual sacrifice.

row.basis: Pursue holiness to see the Lord
row.note: The commentary presents purification as an action that precedes the enduring outcome; Hebrews commands pursuit of holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.

row.basis: Seen things are temporary, unseen things eternal
row.note: The commentary says the hereafter is better and more lasting than present life; Paul contrasts temporary visible things with unseen eternal things.
The commentary makes the person's work matter to the final outcome; Revelation says the dead who die in the Lord are blessed and their deeds follow them.
